definition.text: Disaster recovery is the process of regaining access to infrastructure and systems after a natural disaster, cyber attack or other business disruption.

facts.text: Disaster recovery relies on replicating data and computer processing to an off-premises location that the disaster does not affect.
It assumes the primary site cannot be recovered right away, so it restores data and services to a secondary site.
When servers go down, the business recovers lost data from a second location where it is backed up and, ideally, moves its processing there to keep operating.
Disaster recovery applies policies, tools and procedures to the IT systems behind critical business functions, and is a subset of business continuity.

Disasters come from three broad categories: natural hazards such as floods and earthquakes, technological hazards such as system failures and utility disruptions, and human-caused threats such as cyber attacks, sabotage and war.
Disaster recovery minimizes interruption and downtime, limits damage, speeds restoration and helps retain customers.

Regulators mandate disaster recovery for organizations handling sensitive data; in US healthcare the HIPAA Security Rule requires disaster recovery plans, data backup plans and periodic testing of contingency procedures.
Singh notes that disaster recovery is seldom discussed in system design interviews but is worth a basic understanding.

title: Recovery time objective
article: IT disaster recovery#IT service continuity > Recovery Time Objective

definition.text: The recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable delay between an interruption of service and its restoration.

facts.text: The RTO sets the acceptable window during which a service may be unavailable, that is, how long an application or network can stay offline after a disaster.
In business continuity planning the process owners set the RTO during a business impact analysis, including time frames for alternate or manual workarounds.
The business continuity group runs timed rehearsals to determine and refine the recovery time actual (RTA), the critical metric against which the RTO is checked.
RTO and RPO together measure tolerable performance: time lost from normal business functioning, and data lost or not backed up during that period.
RTO and RPO must be balanced against business risk and the other system design criteria.
Recovery metrics are often used alongside failure metrics: mean time between failures, mean time to first failure, mean time to repair and mean down time.

title: Recovery point objective
article: IT disaster recovery#IT service continuity > Recovery Point Objective

definition.text: The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable amount of time since the last recovery point, that is, the longest interval of data loss tolerated.

facts.text: The RPO fixes what counts as an acceptable loss of data between the last recovery point and the interruption of service.
RPO measures the maximum time in which recent data might be permanently lost, not the quantity of data lost.
If the plan is to restore the last available backup, the RPO is the interval between such backups.
The existing backup regime does not determine the RPO; the business impact analysis determines it for each service.
When the RPO is measured in minutes, off-site mirrored backups must be maintained continuously, because a daily off-site backup will not suffice.
When data must go off-site, the period in which data might be lost may start when backups are prepared, not when they are secured off-site.
A data synchronization point is where a backup is completed; update processing halts during the disk-to-disk copy, and the backup reflects the data as of that copy, not when it reaches tape.
Sending synchronous copies to an offsite mirror allows for most unforeseen events.

definition.text: A disaster recovery strategy is the set of measures chosen to restore systems and data after a disaster, derived from the business continuity plan.

facts.text: The strategy derives from the business continuity plan; a cost-benefit analysis picks the measures, since the right one depends on the cost of downtime compared with the cost of implementing it.
Common strategies are backups to tape sent off-site, backups to disk on-site and copied off-site, and replication off-site; storing data off-site or on a removable drive is the simplest.

Cloud options include private cloud replication of metadata, hybrid cloud replication both on-site and off-site for instant fail-over, high availability systems replicated off-site, and disaster recovery as a service from a third-party vendor.
Precautionary measures include local mirrors and RAID, surge protectors, an uninterruptible power supply or backup generator, fire prevention systems and anti-virus software.

title: Hot, warm and cold sites
article: IT disaster recovery#IT service continuity > Principles of backup sites

definition.text: A backup site is hot if it operates before a disaster, warm if it is ready to begin operating, and cold if it needs substantial work to begin operating.

facts.text: A robust disaster recovery strategy starts from two benchmarks, the recovery time objective and the recovery point objective, and picks a standby tier that meets them.
In a cold site the organization sets up only basic infrastructure in a second site.
A hot site keeps up-to-date copies of data at all times; it is time-consuming to set up and costs more than a cold site, but dramatically reduces downtime.
Backup and restore means regular backups of data and systems; typical RTO runs from several hours to a few days, and RPO from a few hours up to the last successful backup.
Pilot light keeps crucial components ready to activate so it can scale rapidly; typical RTO is a few minutes to several hours, and RPO depends on how often data is synchronized.
Warm standby is a semi-active environment with current data; typical RTO is within a few minutes to hours, and RPO is up to the last few minutes or hours.

A hot site or multi-site configuration is a fully operational duplicate environment running in parallel with the primary; typical RTO is almost immediate, often a few minutes, and RPO is usually a few seconds.

notes: The article anchor covers hot/warm/cold; the four tiers (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site) come from the ByteByteGo cloud-disaster-recovery-strategies guide.

definition.text: Disaster recovery practices are the controls, tests and procedures that keep a recovery plan working when a disaster happens.

facts.text: Controls are preventive, detective or corrective, are recorded in the disaster recovery plan, and are exercised regularly in DR tests that verify the plan and expose weaknesses or gaps.
A cloud recovery strategy should be flexible enough for partial failures, such as recovering specific files, as well as for full environment failures.
Define who may execute the plan and separate those permissions from access to backup data, which limits unauthorized actions; document the plan so operators can follow it under stress.
Planning ahead is cost-effective: every $1 spent on hazard mitigation, such as a disaster recovery plan, saves society $4 in response and recovery costs.

definition.text: High availability architectures pair a node with a standby, secondary or second primary so the service keeps answering when one node fails.

facts.text: In the CAP theorem, availability means every non-failing node can be queried and returns a reasonable response within a reasonable time, with no error or timeout.
A design target of 4-9's means the service is up 99.99% of the time and down at most 52.5 minutes per year.
Availability only guarantees a response, not that the data is the most up-to-date.
In primary-backup, the backup is a stand-by that receives replicated data; on failure the switch to it is manual, and the idle backup may waste hardware.
In primary-secondary, the secondary can serve reads to balance load, but replication latency means reads from it may be inconsistent with the primary.

In primary-primary, both nodes handle reads and writes and replicate to each other, raising throughput; but if both update the same product the final state can be unpredictable, so use it with caution.
Deploying on Amazon EC2, which has 90% availability, a double-node architecture raises availability from 90% to 99%.

definition.text: Observability is the ability to ask arbitrary questions about a system without knowing ahead of time what to ask; logging, tracing and metrics are its three pillars.

facts.text: Logging records discrete events, such as an incoming request or a visit to a database, and has the highest volume of the three pillars.
Teams define a standardized logging format so keywords can be searched across massive logs; the ELK (Elastic-Logstash-Kibana) stack is often used to build a log analysis platform.
Tracing is request-scoped: it follows one user request through the API gateway, load balancer, services and database, which helps identify bottlenecks.
Metrics are aggregatable measurements such as service QPS, API responsiveness and latency, with raw data recorded in time-series databases like InfluxDB.
Prometheus pulls the metrics and transforms them by pre-defined alerting rules; Grafana displays them, and the alert manager sends email, SMS or Slack notifications.
OpenTelemetry unifies the three pillars in a single framework.
Monitoring watches predefined sets of telemetry, whereas observability is based on exploring properties and patterns that were not defined in advance; a monitored system may also be observable.
Metrics are tagged, cardinality-limited measurements that usually represent aggregates, and metrics and logs must be instrumented up front, so an unforeseen issue can require shipping new code.

definition.text: A service level indicator (SLI) is a measure of the service level a provider delivers to a customer.

facts.text: SLIs form the basis of service level objectives, which in turn form the basis of service level agreements; an SLI is also called an SLA metric or service metric.
An SLI is the measured value of the metric an SLO describes; to stay in compliance with the SLA, its value must always meet or exceed the SLO's value.
Common SLIs are latency, throughput, availability and error rate; others include durability for storage systems, end-to-end latency for pipelines, and correctness.
The availability SLI varies with the service's nature and architecture; a simple web service might use the ratio of successful responses to the total valid requests received.

An SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the service level; request latency is the key SLI for most services, and error rate (a fraction of requests) and throughput in requests per second are also common.
SLI measurements are usually aggregated: raw data is collected over a measurement window and turned into a rate, average or percentile.
Ideally an SLI directly measures the service level of interest, but sometimes only a proxy is available; client-side latency matters most to users yet may only be measurable at the server.
Most indicators are gathered on the server side with a monitoring system, but some need client-side collection, since browser page-load problems do not show up in backend latency.

definition.text: A service-level agreement (SLA) is an agreement, typically a binding contract, between a service provider and a customer that sets the quality, availability and responsibilities of a service as contract terms.

facts.text: An SLA defines the promises a company makes to its users about specific metrics such as service availability, and is often written by the company's business or legal team.

SLAs often contain service-level objectives for defined service level indicators, such as mean time between failures, mean time to repair, network throughput, jitter, uptime, first-call resolution and turnaround time.
SLAs, SLOs and SLIs let companies define, track and monitor their promises to users, which builds user trust and drives continuous improvement of incident response.
Unlike traditional contracts, SLAs often require the parties to meet regularly, apply rewards and penalties for performance, and leave room for periodic revision.

Large organizations keep internal SLAs between units, one as customer and one as provider, which keeps quality of service consistent across units and locations and allows comparing an in-house department with an external provider.

SLAs exist at different levels: customer-based for one customer group across all its services, service-based for all customers of a service, and multilevel when one SLA addresses different customer sets in layers.
In outsourcing, SLAs are negotiated upfront in the contract, which may carry financial penalties and a right to terminate if SLA metrics are consistently missed.
SLAs may be supported by operational-level agreements (OLAs).

title: SLA components

definition.text: A well-defined SLA contains the type of service, the desired performance level, monitoring and reporting, steps for reporting issues, response and resolution time frames, and repercussions for missed commitments.

facts.text: It names the type of service and the desired performance level, especially reliability (minimal disruption, available almost always) and responsiveness (acting promptly after a request).
It describes how performance is monitored: which statistics are gathered, how often, and how customers can access them.
It gives contact details and the order for reporting a problem; the response time frame is when the provider starts investigating, and the resolution time frame is when the issue is fixed.
If the provider misses its commitments, the customer may have the right to terminate the contract or ask for a refund for losses from the service failure.

notes: Components follow Dinesh Verma's list as given in the Wikipedia section.

definition.text: Cloud SLAs are service-based agreements that cover a shared infrastructure rather than agreements with one customer.

facts.text: Because cloud resources are shared, SLAs span the cloud and are offered by providers as service-based rather than customer-based agreements.

Cloud performance is measured and reported from the end user's ability to consume resources; cloud SLAs focus on data center characteristics and, more recently, network characteristics to support end-to-end SLAs.

The downside of the cloud is that the complex environment makes the root cause of service interruptions hard to determine, yet applications moved there must reach the same or more demanding service levels.
Any SLA management strategy has two phases: negotiating the contract and monitoring its fulfillment in real time.

definition.text: A service-level objective (SLO) is a target value or range of values for a service level, measured by a service level indicator.

facts.text: An SLO is a key element of an SLA, an individual promise within it, and the specific goal the service must meet to comply; typical SLOs cover availability, throughput, frequency, response time or quality.
SLOs give a quantitative definition of the service level a customer can expect, and are agreed to measure the provider's performance and avoid disputes from misunderstanding.
In simple terms, SLOs are targets for how often a service may fail or not operate properly while users are still not meaningfully upset.
SLOs are formed by setting goals for SLIs; an availability SLO may be the expected value of an availability SLI over a prescribed duration, for example four weeks.
An SLO should state an achievement value, a target measurement, a measurement period, and where and how it is measured, for example 90% of helpdesk calls answered in under 20 seconds over one month.
Example SLOs include an application available 99.95% of the time over a year, and 85% of TCP replies within 1.5 seconds and 99.5% within 4 seconds over a month.
SLOs should always be simple, clearly defined and easy to measure, so it is clear whether the objective is being met.
Companies may also set internal SLOs for internal services that depend on each other, especially those practicing site reliability engineering.

definition.text: Site reliability engineering (SRE) is a discipline that applies software engineering to IT infrastructure and operations to monitor and improve the availability and performance of deployed software systems.

facts.text: SREs are responsible for a combination of availability, latency, performance, efficiency, change management, monitoring, emergency response and capacity planning.
SRE focuses on automation, system design and improved resilience, typically with an infrastructure as code methodology.
SRE is considered a specific implementation of DevOps that concentrates on building reliable systems, while DevOps covers a broader scope of operations.

Common practices include automating repetitive tasks, defining reliability goals to prevent endless effort, designing systems to reduce risks to availability, latency and efficiency, and observability.
Toil management is a principle: toil is manual, repetitive, automatable operational work.
Reliability goals are defined and measured with SLIs, SLOs and error budgets.
Other principles are defining, testing and running an incident management process, and change and release management including CI/CD.

definition.text: SRE teams are organized in several models: kitchen sink, infrastructure, product or application, embedded and consulting.

facts.text: A kitchen sink team oversees an expansive, often unbounded scope, including performance optimization, incident management and automation.
Infrastructure SRE teams keep the systems that support other teams' workflows up, fast and efficient, while platform teams develop the software and systems used across the organization.
Product or application SRE teams are dedicated to specific products, and large companies typically have several, each focusing on different products or applications.

In the embedded model, individual SREs or pairs join software engineering teams to apply automation, monitoring and incident response; consulting SRE teams instead advise organizations on adopting SRE practices.

definition.text: Business continuity planning is the process of creating systems of prevention and recovery to deal with potential threats, so an organization can keep delivering products or services at acceptable levels after a disruptive incident.

facts.text: Business continuity is the intended outcome of properly executing both business continuity planning and disaster recovery; planning aims to keep operations running before and during disaster recovery.

Business continuity planning is a subset of risk management; any event that could hurt operations belongs in the plan, such as supply chain interruption or loss of critical infrastructure, including computing and network resources.
A plan outlines a range of disaster scenarios and the steps the business takes in each to return to regular trade; it is written ahead of time and can include precautions.
Continuity need not cover every activity; ISO 22301 requires organizations to define continuity objectives, the minimum acceptable service levels and the maximum tolerable period of disruption.

Plans are tested with tabletop exercises (a few people on one aspect), medium exercises (several teams, with pre-scripted surprises) and complex exercises (no-notice activation, actual evacuation and use of a recovery site).

The plan needs regular maintenance: confirming the manual and training staff, and testing technical solutions and recovery procedures, including that staff can recover within the recovery time objective.

title: Business impact analysis
article: Business continuity planning#Analysis > Business impact analysis (BIA)

definition.text: A business impact analysis identifies and evaluates the effects of disruptions on operations and determines the recovery priorities and strategies the organization needs.

facts.text: It identifies critical activities and their dependencies (people, processes, vendors, technology, facilities) and assesses the financial, operational, reputational and legal impact of disruption.

For each function it assigns a recovery point objective, the acceptable data loss (for example, whether losing 2 days of data is acceptable), and a recovery time objective, the acceptable time to restore the function.

The longest key services can be unavailable before stakeholders see unacceptable consequences is the maximum tolerable period of disruption, also called maximum acceptable outage; ISO 22301 defines these two terms identically.

When several systems crash, recovery must also balance data consistency against RTO and RPO; the recovery consistency objective is a percentage measuring deviation of business data across systems, where 100% means none.

definition.text: Disaster recovery tiers grade recovery solutions from no off-site data up to highly automated recovery, from SHARE's seven tiers of 1992 that IBM updated to eight in 2012.

facts.text: Tier 0 has no off-site data or recovery plan, so recovery may be impossible; Tier 1 keeps off-site backups but no systems to restore them on, accepting days to weeks of data loss.
Tier 2 adds a hot site to restore tape backups, still recreating hours to days of data; Tier 3 also electronically vaults mission-critical data, which is more current than shipped tapes.

Tier 4 uses disk-based point-in-time copies for fresher data and faster recovery; Tier 5 keeps data consistent between production and recovery data centers, with little or no loss depending on the application.

Tier 6 keeps data current with little or no loss and does not depend on applications for consistency; Tier 7 adds automated application recovery, restoring systems faster and more reliably than manual procedures.

definition.text: Incident management is the process of limiting the disruption an incident could cause to operations, services or functions, followed by a return to business as usual.

facts.text: Incident management identifies, analyzes and corrects hazards to prevent recurrence; left unmanaged, an incident can escalate into an emergency, crisis or disaster.

Incidents are handled by an incident response or incident management team, designated beforehand or during the event and put in control to restore normal functions; an incident commander leads the response.
Frameworks follow a lifecycle of detection, classification, response coordination, containment, recovery and post-incident review.
In IT service management the first goal is restoring normal service operation, meaning service within the SLA, as quickly as possible while minimizing business impact.
Post-incident analysis determines why the incident happened despite precautions, and its findings feed back into policy and its practical implementation.

Root cause analysis should assess human factors: an active failure has immediate effects, while latent failures come from high-level decisions and lie dormant until a triggering event combines with them.
Typical challenges are growing alert and event noise, a lengthy problem resolution process, and inability to predict and prevent service degradations or outages.
For computer security incidents, a computer security incident response team analyzes the situation, determines how far an intrusion reached and takes corrective action.

definition.text: Chaos engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system to build confidence that it can withstand turbulent conditions in production.

facts.text: Resilience, the ability to tolerate failures while keeping quality of service, is usually a requirement that teams miss for lack of time or domain knowledge; chaos engineering encompasses techniques for meeting it.
It can build resilience against infrastructure failures, network failures and application failures, including unhandled exceptions.
Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly picks a server and disables it during normal working hours, so engineers must build redundancy and automation that survive such failures without affecting users.
The intent is to move from assuming no breakdowns to treating breakdowns as inevitable, making built-in resilience an obligation rather than an option.
The Simian Army extends the idea: Chaos Gorilla drops a whole availability zone and Chaos Kong drops an entire region, to test response and recovery to rarer large-scale failures.
Game days purposely create major failures on a regular basis to raise reliability, inspired by firefighter training; Google's DiRT does the same for disaster recovery testing.
Operational readiness can be evaluated with chaos simulations; one Kubernetes experiment terminated random pods and used the pods' recovery time as the resiliency metric.

definition.text: A backup is a copy of computer data taken and stored elsewhere so it can be used to restore the original after a data loss event.

facts.text: Backups recover data lost to deletion or corruption, or data from an earlier time; they are a simple form of disaster recovery, though not every backup system can rebuild a cluster or database server.
A backup system holds at least one copy of all data worth saving, in a repository that aggregates backups of the data sources.
Backup differs from replication in that the saved copy of data remains unchanged for a long period of time.

The recovery point objective is the maximum targeted period in which data might be lost, and a more recent point needs more frequent syncing to the repository; the recovery time objective is the time from disaster to restoration.
Backup storage can be online (a restore starts in milliseconds), near-line, off-line (immune to online failure modes) or sent off-site to a vault to protect against site-specific disasters.
Deduplication stores one copy of redundant data at file or block level, on the client before transfer (saving bandwidth) or at the target device; compression also shrinks the data stored.
Encrypting backup media mitigates loss or theft, but encryption is CPU intensive and only as secure as the key management policy.
Checksum or hash validation verifies that data was copied accurately, and dry runs can validate that the backed-up data is reliable.

definition.text: Backup methods differ in what each backup copies: complete data, changes since the last full backup, changes since the last backup of any kind, or every change as it happens.

facts.text: A full backup holds complete copies of the source data at specific points in time; system images record known good configurations but suit deploying a standard setup more than ongoing backup.

An incremental backup stores only data changed since a reference point, usually a full backup; a restore starts from the last full backup and applies the incrementals, and some systems build a synthetic full from them.
A differential backup saves data changed since the last full backup, so a restore needs at most two backups, but each differential takes longer as changes accumulate.
Incrementals copy changes since the most recent backup of any type, while differentials copy changes since the last full backup, whatever differentials came between.
A reverse incremental keeps a recent mirror of the source plus the differences needed to rebuild earlier states, by periodically synchronizing the full backup with the live copy.

Continuous data protection instantly saves every change and allows restoring to any point in time; near-CDP takes incremental backups at intervals such as every 15 minutes, so restores only reach an interval boundary.
An unstructured repository is a stack of media with minimal information about what was backed up; it is the easiest to implement but unlikely to be highly recoverable because it lacks automation.

definition.text: The 3-2-1 rule says to keep at least 3 copies of the data, on 2 different types of storage media, with one copy offsite in a remote location.

facts.text: Using two or more different media avoids losses with similar causes; optical discs may survive being underwater while LTO tapes may not, and SSDs cannot suffer head crashes.
An offsite copy, which can be cloud storage, protects against fire, theft of physical media and natural disasters such as floods and earthquakes.
No storage is perfect, so many experts keep a second local physical copy even with an offsite one; physically protected drives resist fire only for a limited time.
Ransomware can overwrite a backup drive that stays plugged in and accessible, so at least one backup medium should be disconnected when not in use.

title: Backing up live data
article: Backup#Selection and extraction of data > Live data

definition.text: Files being actively updated are hard to back up consistently; one way is to quiesce them, take a snapshot, resume live operations and back up the snapshot.

facts.text: A snapshot is an instantaneous filesystem function that presents a copy as if frozen at one point in time, often through a copy-on-write mechanism.

Snapshotting a file while it changes yields a corrupted file, as does doing so across interrelated files such as a database; a fuzzy backup looks successful but does not show the data at a single point in time.
A database hot backup combines a snapshot of the data files with a snapshotted log of changes made during the backup; a restore applies the log to bring the copy up to when the backup ended.
Genuinely high-availability interactive applications can only be backed up with continuous data protection.

title: Choosing service level indicators
article: doc>sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives#What Do You and Your Users Care About?

definition.text: Choosing indicators means selecting a handful of metrics that reflect what users want from the system, rather than every metric a monitoring system can track.

facts.text: Too many indicators make it hard to pay attention to those that matter, while too few leave significant behaviors unexamined.
Serving systems usually care about availability, latency and throughput; storage systems about latency, availability and durability; big data pipelines about throughput and end-to-end latency.
All systems should track correctness as an indicator of health, though it is often a property of the data rather than the infrastructure and so usually not an SRE responsibility.
Aggregation needs care: averaging requests over a minute may hide much higher instantaneous request rates in bursts that last only a few seconds.
Standardizing SLI definitions (aggregation interval, aggregation region, measurement frequency, which requests count) avoids reasoning from first principles each time.

definition.text: Choosing SLO targets is not a purely technical activity, because product and business implications shape the SLIs and SLOs, and SRE advises on the risks and viability of options.

facts.text: Start from what users care about, not what is easy to measure, approximating their needs if necessary; working backward from desired objectives to indicators often works better than the reverse.
Do not pick a target from current performance: adopting values without reflection can lock you into a system that needs heroic efforts to meet its targets and cannot improve without redesign.
Have as few SLOs as possible, just enough to cover the system's attributes, and defend each one: an SLO that never wins a conversation about priorities is probably not worth having.
Avoid absolutes: demanding a system that is always available and scales without added latency is unrealistic, costly to operate and probably better than users would be happy with.
Perfection can wait: it is better to start with a loose target and tighten it than to set an overly strict one that must be relaxed once found unattainable.
SLOs should drive prioritization for SREs and developers; a good SLO is a legitimate forcing function, but an overly aggressive one wastes heroic effort and a lax one yields a bad product.

definition.text: Publishing SLOs sets expectations for system behavior, so users can tell whether a service fits their use case.

facts.text: A team building a photo-sharing site might avoid a service promising strong durability and low cost for slightly lower availability, though it could suit an archival records system.

Keeping an internal SLO tighter than the advertised one leaves room to respond to chronic problems before users see them and to accept reimplementations that trade performance for cost or maintainability.

Do not overachieve: users build on what a service actually delivers, so performing far above its SLO breeds over-dependence; remedies include planned outages, throttling some requests, or designs that are not faster under light load.
Knowing how well a system meets expectations guides whether to invest in speed, availability and resilience, or spend time on technical debt and new features.

definition.text: An error budget is the rate at which a service may miss its SLOs, giving an objective measure of how unreliable the service is allowed to be within a period.

facts.text: Insisting on meeting SLOs 100% of the time slows innovation and deployment and needs costly, overly conservative solutions, so an error budget allows a rate of misses, tracked daily or weekly; it is an SLO for meeting other SLOs.

Product management defines an SLO, a neutral monitoring system measures actual uptime, and the difference is the unreliability budget left for the quarter; while budget remains, new releases can be pushed.
With an SLO of serving 99.999% of queries per quarter, the error budget is a 0.001% failure rate; a problem failing 0.0002% of expected queries spends 20% of the quarterly budget.
Developers are judged on velocity and SREs on reliability, so they pull in opposite directions; the budget is an objective agreed metric that removes politics and gives both a common incentive.

As a control loop on release velocity, releases continue while SLOs are met and halt when the budget is spent, while testing and resilience work is added; subtler options slow releases or roll them back.
A large budget lets developers take more risk; a nearly drained one makes them push for more testing themselves, provided the SRE team has authority to stop launches when the SLO is broken.
Network outages and datacenter failures also consume the budget and may reduce pushes for the rest of the quarter; a team struggling to launch features may loosen the SLO to enlarge the budget.

definition.text: Past a certain point, increasing a service's reliability makes things worse for the service and its users, because extreme reliability limits feature development and delivery and sharply raises cost.

facts.text: Users usually cannot tell high reliability from extreme reliability, because other components like the cellular network dominate their experience: a user on a 99% reliable smartphone cannot tell 99.99% from 99.999%.
Cost does not rise linearly with reliability: an incremental improvement in reliability may cost 100x more than the previous increment.

The cost has two dimensions: redundant machines and equipment (for maintenance windows or parity blocks), and the opportunity cost of engineers reducing risk instead of building user-visible features.
SRE manages reliability by managing risk as a continuum, weighing cost against benefit per service and aligning the risk a service takes with the risk the business is willing to bear.

The goal is reliable enough but no more: an availability target such as 99.99% is both a minimum and a maximum, since exceeding it by much wastes chances to add features, clean up technical debt or cut costs.

definition.text: Request-based availability defines availability as the proportion of requests that succeed over a rolling window, instead of the proportion of time a system is up.

facts.text: Time-based availability counts uptime: a 99.99% target allows up to 52.56 minutes of downtime a year, but for globally distributed services some traffic is almost always served somewhere, so uptime is rarely meaningful.
A system serving 2.5M requests a day with a 99.99% daily target can serve up to 250 errors and still meet it.
Not all requests are equal, but the success rate over all requests approximates unplanned downtime as the end user sees it, and suits systems that do not serve end users directly.
Batch systems can use it too, counting records processed successfully and unsuccessfully; targets are typically set quarterly and tracked weekly or even daily.

title: Setting an availability target
article: doc>sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk#Identifying the Risk Tolerance of Consumer Services

definition.text: A service's availability target depends on its function and market position: what users expect, whether it ties to revenue, whether it is paid or free, what competitors offer, and whether it serves consumers or enterprises.

facts.text: An enterprise service might get an external quarterly target of 99.9% backed by a stronger internal target and penalty contract, while a fast-growing consumer product can take a lower target because feature speed matters more.
Cost is often the key factor: ask what extra revenue one more nine would bring and whether it offsets the cost; raising a $1M-revenue service from 99.9% to 99.99% is worth $900.
Without a revenue translation, a yardstick is the background error rate of ISPs, measured between 0.01% and 1%; errors driven below it fall within the noise of a user's Internet connection.

The shape of failures matters: a constant low failure rate and an occasional full outage may produce the same error count but different business impact, and scheduled maintenance windows can count as planned downtime.

title: Multiple service levels for infrastructure
article: doc>sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk#Identifying the Risk Tolerance of Infrastructure Services

definition.text: Infrastructure has multiple clients with varying needs, so a cost-effective answer is to partition it and offer it at multiple independent levels of service.

facts.text: Clients of a shared storage system can want opposite things: low-latency users want empty request queues, while offline-analysis users want queues never empty so the system never idles.
Low-latency clusters carry substantial slack capacity for short queues and isolation, while throughput clusters run hot with less redundancy, perhaps at as little as 10-50% of the cost.

Explicit levels of service expose the cost of each level so clients pick the cheapest that meets their needs, for example a globally consistent store for critical data and a cheaper eventually consistent one for optional data.
Different service classes can run on identical hardware and software, varying resource quantities, redundancy, geographic provisioning and software configuration.

definition.text: Monitoring is collecting, processing, aggregating and displaying real-time quantitative data about a system, such as query counts and types, error counts and types, processing times and server lifetimes.

facts.text: Reasons to monitor include analyzing long-term trends, comparing over time or between experiment groups, alerting when something is or will soon be broken, building dashboards, and ad hoc debugging.
A dashboard is a prebuilt summary view of a service's core metrics, normally including the four golden signals; alerts are notifications for humans, classified as tickets, email alerts and pages.
Monitoring and alerting lets a system say when it is broken or about to break; when it cannot fix itself, a human investigates, mitigates and finds the root cause.
Monitoring a complex application is a significant engineering effort, yet SRE teams avoid any situation that requires someone to stare at a screen to watch for problems.

Simpler and faster monitoring with better post hoc analysis works best, avoiding magic systems that learn thresholds or detect causality; monitoring that grows complex becomes fragile and a maintenance burden.
Rules that catch real incidents most often should be simple, predictable and reliable; rarely exercised configuration, and signals that no dashboard or alert uses, are candidates for removal.

Choose measurement granularity to fit the goal: probing a 99.9% service more than once or twice a minute is probably unnecessary, and costly per-second CPU readings can be sampled on the server and aggregated into buckets.

definition.text: The four golden signals of monitoring are latency, traffic, errors and saturation; if you can measure only four metrics of a user-facing system, measure these.

facts.text: Latency is the time to service a request; track successful and failed requests separately, since a fast HTTP 500 skews the figures, and note that a slow error is worse than a fast one.

Traffic measures demand in a system-specific metric: HTTP requests per second for a web service, network I/O or concurrent sessions for audio streaming, transactions and retrievals per second for a key-value store.

Errors are requests that fail explicitly (HTTP 500s), implicitly (an HTTP 200 with wrong content) or by policy (slower than a committed one-second response); load balancer 500s catch total failures, but only end-to-end tests catch wrong content.
Saturation is how full the service is, emphasizing the most constrained resource; many systems degrade before reaching 100% utilization, so a utilization target is essential.
Rising latency is often a leading indicator of saturation, and the 99th percentile response time over a small window such as one minute can give a very early signal.
Saturation also covers prediction of impending saturation, such as a database that will fill its hard drive in 4 hours.
If you measure all four signals and page a human when one is problematic (or, for saturation, nearly so), the service is at least decently covered by monitoring.

definition.text: Black-box monitoring tests externally visible behavior as a user would see it, while white-box monitoring uses metrics exposed by the system's internals, such as logs or an HTTP handler emitting statistics.

facts.text: Black-box monitoring is symptom-oriented and catches active problems; white-box monitoring inspects internals through instrumentation, so it can detect imminent problems and failures masked by retries.
Black-box monitoring suits paging because it only bothers a human when a problem is already ongoing and causing real symptoms, but it is fairly useless for imminent problems.

White-box monitoring is essential for debugging telemetry: you need to know how fast the web server sees the database and how fast the database sees itself, to tell a slow database from a network problem.
In a multilayered system one person's symptom is another's cause: slow database reads are a symptom for the database SRE but a cause for the frontend SRE watching a slow website.

license.name: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
license.evidence: footer of sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/: Licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0

definition.text: Good alerting pages a human only for an urgent, actionable condition that is actively or imminently user-visible, giving good signal and very low noise.

facts.text: Monitoring should answer what is broken (the symptom) and why (a possibly intermediate cause); keeping the two apart is key to monitoring with maximum signal and minimum noise.
Paging a human is expensive, interrupting work or sleep; when pages are too frequent, people skim or ignore them, even a real one masked by noise, and outages can be prolonged.
Every page should be actionable, need intelligence rather than a robotic response, and concern a novel problem; people can react with urgency only a few times a day before becoming fatigued.

Before adding an alert, ask whether it could ever be ignored as benign, whether it definitely means users are affected, whether action is possible, urgent or automatable, and whether others are already paged.
Put effort into catching symptoms rather than causes, worrying only about very definite, very imminent causes; never alert merely because something seems a bit weird.
Email alerts are of very limited value and quickly overrun with noise; favor a dashboard of ongoing subcritical problems, possibly paired with a log for historical correlations.
Pages with rote responses are a red flag: when an alert becomes frequent, remove its root cause or fully automate the response, since every page distracts a human from improving the system.

In one over-alerting case, an SLO based on mean latency was dominated by a long tail and alerts fired constantly; the team eased it to 75th percentile latency and disabled email alerts to gain time to fix causes.

definition.text: Data integrity means that services remain accessible to users with accurate data, because to users data loss, corruption and extended unavailability look the same.

facts.text: Data integrity is the accuracy and consistency of data over its lifetime, but from the user's point of view integrity without expected, regular availability is effectively the same as having no data.

Because loss, corruption and extended unavailability are indistinguishable to users, integrity applies to all types of data in all services; Google suggests 24 hours as a starting threshold for unavailability that is too long.

Each service has independent uptime and integrity requirements: a 99.99% uptime SLO allows about an hour of downtime a year, but 99.99% good bytes in a 2 GB artifact means up to 200 KB garbled, which is catastrophic.
The secret to superior integrity is proactive detection plus rapid repair and recovery: a corrupted artifact detected and fixed within half an hour still leaves it 99.99% available that year.
Integrity is the means and data availability the goal, so SRE sets concrete objectives with measurable indicators and proves systems can maintain availability with a predicted maximum downtime.
Strategies for detection, repair and recovery trade uptime against integrity, and the right mix depends on how an application balances uptime, latency, scale, velocity and privacy.

title: Defense in depth for data integrity
article: doc>sre.google/sre-book/data-integrity#The 24 Combinations of Data Integrity Failure Modes

definition.text: Defense in depth protects data with multiple layers, each guarding against progressively less common loss scenarios, because no silver bullet covers the many combinations of failure modes.

facts.text: The first layer is soft deletion, the second is backups and their recovery methods, and the third is regular data validation for early detection.
Replication cuts across all layers and is occasionally useful for recovery in specific scenarios, but data recovery plans should not rely on it.

Even a bulletproof system is susceptible to bugs and operator error, so services must detect integrity issues quickly for them to be fixable, and protection mechanisms must be assumed able to fail too.
Large-scale integrity needs several complementary but uncoupled practices, each offering a high degree of protection on its own.
Having many disks and a fast network for replication does not remove the need for layers, because multiple layers guard against breakdown or compromise of any single protection mechanism.

license.evidence: footer of sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/: Licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0

definition.text: Soft deletion marks deleted data immediately, making it unusable except by the application's administrative code paths, and destroys it after a reasonable delay.

facts.text: When velocity is high and privacy matters, application bugs cause most data loss and corruption, so being able to undelete data for a limited time becomes the primary defense against permanent inadvertent loss.
Soft deletion happens when a user empties the trash, and a support tool lets authorized administrators undelete items; it also helps against account hijackers who delete the original user's data.

The delay before destruction depends on policy, law, storage cost and pricing; common choices are 15, 30, 45 or 60 days, and since most hijacking and integrity issues surface within 60 days, longer delays have a weak case.

Lazy deletion is soft deletion controlled by the storage system: deleted data becomes inaccessible to the application but is kept up to a few weeks; it is costly for short-lived data and impractical where destruction deadlines must be guaranteed.
A trash folder is the primary defense against user error; soft deletion is primary against developer error and secondary against user error; lazy deletion is primary against internal developer error.

The most devastating deletions come from developers unfamiliar with deletion-related code, especially batch pipelines, so interfaces should hinder bypassing soft deletion, for example with built-in, enabled soft deletion and undeletion APIs.

Revision history helps with some corruption but not most accidental deletion, since some implementations remove prior states on deletion; apply soft or lazy deletion principles to revision history too.

definition.text: The most important difference between backups and archives is that backups can be loaded back into an application while archives cannot, so a backup effort should focus on data recovery.

facts.text: Archives safekeep data for long periods to meet auditing, discovery and compliance needs, and need not recover within service uptime limits; a week to retrieve logs for a month-long audit may be acceptable.
Real backups must be recovered quickly, well within the service's uptime needs, or users lose useful access from the onset of the problem until recovery completes.
Because recent data is at risk until safely backed up, real backups may run daily, hourly or more often, so weigh how fast you must recover and how much recent data you can afford to lose.
People do not want backups, they want restores, so teams define SLOs for data availability across failure modes and practice demonstrating they can meet them.

title: Tiered backup strategy
article: doc>sre.google/sre-book/data-integrity#Second Layer: Backups and Their Related Recovery Methods

definition.text: A tiered backup strategy keeps frequent, quickly restored backups near the live datastores and fewer, longer-retained backups on more remote, more independent storage.

facts.text: Backups do not matter, recovery does: the scenarios you must recover from should dictate the backup method, how often you take full or incremental restore points, where you store backups and how long you keep them.
The less recent data you can lose, the more serious an incremental strategy should be; frequent full backups burden live datastores, so take fulls off-peak and incrementals when busy.

The faster users must be rescued, the more local backups should be: costly quick-restore snapshots kept briefly in the storage instance, newer backups on distributed storage nearby, then nearline or offline storage for longer.

Reaching back as far as possible helps with low-grade corruption bugs found months later, but costs more and old backups may be unusable after code and schema changes; Google drew the line between 30 and 90 days.

The first tier holds many frequent, quickly restored backups near the live data, retained hours to single-digit days and restored in minutes, protecting against most software bugs and developer error.

The second tier holds fewer backups for single-digit or low double-digit days on local distributed filesystems, restoring in hours, covering storage-technology mishaps and bugs found too late for the first tier.
Later tiers use nearline tape libraries and offsite media against site-level issues; moving large data between tiers is expensive, so these backups are taken less often but retained longer.

title: Replication is not backup
article: doc>sre.google/sre-book/data-integrity#Challenges of Maintaining Data Integrity Deep and Wide

definition.text: Replication is not recoverability: datastores that automatically sync replicas push a corrupt row or errant delete to every copy, likely before the problem can be isolated.

facts.text: Replication gives data locality and protection from a site-specific disaster, but cannot protect against many sources of data loss, so it is a flawed answer to being asked whether you have a backup.
Nonserving copies in another format, such as frequent database exports, guard against user errors and application bugs but not lower-layer losses, and add risk of bugs in data conversion.
Diversity is key: protecting against failure at one layer needs data on diverse components at that layer, and media isolation helps because a disk driver bug is unlikely to affect tape drives.

Data freshness and restore speed compete with comprehensive protection: replication takes seconds, exporting a database snapshot to the filesystem about 40 minutes, and a full filesystem backup hours, with restores about as slow.

Ideally every storage instance, backups included, is replicated; where that is infeasible, stagger backups across independently failing sites and write them with redundancy such as RAID, Reed-Solomon codes or GFS-style replication.

title: Point-in-time recovery
article: doc>sre.google/sre-book/data-integrity#Types of Failures That Lead to Data Loss

definition.text: Point-in-time recovery restores each affected artifact to its own unique point in time, possibly for millions of users across days, weeks or months; Google calls it time-travel.

facts.text: A backup and recovery solution giving point-in-time recovery across ACID and BASE datastores while meeting strict uptime, latency, scale, velocity and cost goals is a chimera today, and building it yourself costs velocity.
Many projects compromise with a tiered backup strategy without it, such as days of costly local snapshots plus full and incremental copies every two days; if you can have both, use both.
Gradual losses may take days to notice, so recovery needs snapshots from further back, and merging restored data with the current state significantly complicates the restore.

title: Data loss failure modes
article: doc>sre.google/sre-book/data-integrity#Types of Failures That Lead to Data Loss

definition.text: Data loss failures vary in root cause, scope and rate, giving 24 distinct types that a data integrity program should consider and a restore plan must handle in any combination.

facts.text: An unrecoverable loss may come from user action, operator error, application bugs, infrastructure defects, faulty hardware or site catastrophes.
Losses may be widespread or narrow, hitting a small subset of users, and either big bang (1 million rows replaced by 10 in a minute) or creeping (10 rows deleted every minute for weeks).
A strategy that guards against a creeping application bug may be useless when a colocation datacenter catches fire.

A study of 19 recovery efforts at Google found the most common user-visible losses involved deletion or lost referential integrity from software bugs, and the hardest were low-grade corruption found weeks or months later.

title: Out-of-band data validation
article: doc>sre.google/sre-book/data-integrity#Third Layer: Early Detection > Out-of-band data validation

definition.text: Out-of-band data validation is a system of checks and balances within and between an application's datastores that detects low-grade corruption or loss before it becomes unrecoverable.

facts.text: Bad data propagates, with references to missing or corrupt data copied and links fanning out, so the sooner a loss is known the easier and more complete recovery is.
Even consensus-based storage is not infallible in practice, so applications cannot know all their data is good until they check: trust storage systems, but verify.
Validation pipelines are often map-reduce or Hadoop jobs; they slow engineering in the short term but give developers courage to move faster later, much as unit tests do.

Validators must be balanced: too strict and engineers abandon them, too lax and corruption slips through, so validate only invariants whose failure devastates users, such as file contents matching folder listings.
Validators that also fix inconsistencies automatically turn emergencies into business as usual.
Validators are costly at scale: they use compute and lower cache hit rates, so they need rate-limiting knobs, and the largest can be sharded to validate one shard per day.
Tiering helps: keep daily validators catching the most disastrous scenarios within 24 hours, and run more rigorous validation less often to contain cost and latency.

Effective validation needs job management, monitoring, rate limiting, troubleshooting tools, playbooks and validation APIs, so a central team should provide the framework while product teams own the business logic.

definition.text: Recovery dependencies, mostly backups, can be latently broken without anyone knowing until recovery is attempted, so recovery must be tested continuously.

facts.text: Finding a broken restore process before you need it lets you take another backup, provision more resources or change the SLO.
Test recovery continuously as part of normal operations and alert when a recovery process stops sending a heartbeat of success; only a full end-to-end test is proof enough.
You only know you can recover your recent state if you actually do so; manual staged tests become drudgery, so automate them and run them continuously.

Confirm that backups are valid and not empty, that resources suffice for setup, restore and post-processing, that recovery finishes in reasonable time, that progress is observable, and that no critical dependency lies outside your control.
Components not continually exercised fail when you need them most, so regular tests make failures happen before a real catastrophe, when problems can be fixed without harm.

facts.text: Gmail lost a significant amount of user data despite many safeguards, internal checks and redundancies, and the loss went beyond what its internal recovery means could restore.
It was the first large-scale use of GTape, Gmail's global offline tape backup, to restore live customer data, though similar restores had been simulated many times.

Thanks to those simulations the team estimated how long the restore would take, restored all accounts within several hours of the estimate, and recovered 99%+ of the data before the estimated completion time.

Backing up an online system gives defense in depth at two layers: against failure of internal redundancy and backup subsystems, and against a wide failure or zero-day in a device driver or filesystem under the disks.
Large disk and network resources for replication did not remove the need for a tape layer, because multiple layers guard against breakdown or compromise of any single protection mechanism.
The smooth recovery relied on a central plan, the product of regular dress rehearsals and dry runs, with many teams, even unrelated ones, pitching in.
Failures are treated as inevitable, so planning covers foreseeable failures and some amount of random, undifferentiated breakage as well.

facts.text: A redesigned, more efficient data deletion pipeline wrongly removed about 600,000 audio references affecting 21,000 users; the damage was found over a month after its first run.
The team disabled the pipeline, then split up: SREs recovered data from offsite tape while developers hunted the root cause, since recovery would be in vain until the bug was fixed.
The recovery came weeks after the annual disaster recovery testing exercise, so the tape team knew its subsystems' limits and had a tool tested in that exercise.
Recovering the tracks meant recalling over 5,000 tapes, split into 5,475 restore jobs that SRE requested programmatically, since a person typing one restore a minute would need over three days.

The 1.5 petabyte first wave ran past its two-day estimate, with 17 bad tapes and 1,862 tapes a vendor omitted; redundant encoding let the team recall redundancy tapes, and users had the tracks back in just short of 7 days.

About 161,000 tracks were deleted before being backed up; store-bought and promotional ones were reinstated from original copies, while user-uploaded files were re-uploaded by clients over more than a week.
The root cause was a race condition: stages designed to run in strict succession slowed as data grew, the timing assumption failed for more data, and wrong data was deleted nondeterministically.

The pipeline was redesigned to remove the race, and monitoring was enhanced to catch runaway deletion bugs before users notice, for example alerting on the global deletion rate crossing an extreme threshold such as 10x the 95th percentile.

definition.text: Borg is a distributed cluster operating system that runs users' jobs, either long-running servers or batch processes, as sets of identical tasks on a cluster's machines.

facts.text: Hardware failures are frequent, with thousands of machines and thousands of disks failing in a typical cluster-year, so software abstracts these failures away from users and service teams.
Machines can run any server, with none dedicated to a program; Borg finds machines for a job's tasks, monitors them, and kills and restarts a malfunctioning task, possibly on a different machine.
Because tasks move between machines, clients reach them through a naming service that resolves a name and task index to an IP address and port, an extra level of indirection.

Each job declares its resource needs, such as 3 CPU cores and 2 GiB of RAM; Borg bin-packs tasks onto machines accounting for failure domains such as racks, and kills and restarts a task that exceeds its request.

definition.text: Sizing a service divides expected peak load by what one task can handle, then adds spare tasks so peak load is still served during updates and machine failures (N+2).

facts.text: With about 100 QPS per task and an expected peak of about 3,470 QPS, at least 35 tasks are needed; N+2 raises this to 37, since an update plus a machine failure could otherwise leave only 35.
N+2 assumes two simultaneous task failures are negligible; single points of failure such as top-of-rack switches or power distribution may invalidate that assumption elsewhere.
Backends are placed per region with N+2, for example 17 tasks in the USA, 16 in Europe and 6 in Asia; South America uses 4 at N+1, saving 20% of hardware for a small risk of higher latency.
The Bigtable is replicated in each region for resilience and lower data-access latency; eventual consistency is acceptable because the content is updated rarely.

definition.text: A user request to a large serving stack passes through DNS, a global load balancer, a reverse-proxy frontend, application frontend and backend servers, and a storage layer such as Bigtable before the reply is assembled.

facts.text: DNS resolution ends at Google's DNS server, which consults GSLB; because GSLB tracks load among frontend servers across regions, it picks the server IP address returned to the user.

The browser connects to the Google Frontend, a reverse proxy that terminates the TCP connection and looks up the service, then uses GSLB to find an available service frontend and sends it an RPC with the HTTP request.
The frontend builds a protobuf request and asks GSLB for an unloaded backend, which reads Bigtable; the reply travels back and the frontend assembles the HTML, all in a few hundred milliseconds.
Many moving parts mean many potential points of failure, and a failing GSLB would wreak havoc; rigorous testing, careful rollout and graceful degradation keep the service reliable.

title: Virtual IP load balancing
article: doc>sre.google/sre-book/load-balancing-frontend#Load Balancing at the Virtual IP Address

definition.text: A virtual IP address is shared across many devices rather than assigned to one network interface, so users see one regular IP address while a network load balancer forwards packets to a machine behind it.

facts.text: A VIP hides implementation details such as the number of machines behind it, and lets operators schedule upgrades or add machines to the pool without users knowing.
Always picking the least loaded backend breaks down for stateful protocols, which need the same backend for a whole connection, forcing the balancer to track every connection passing through it.
The stateless alternative hashes parts of a packet into a connection ID and selects the backend from it, so all packets of a connection reach the same backend without stored state.
With the ID taken modulo the number of backends N, removing one backend changes N to N-1 and remaps almost every packet, resetting nearly all connections when backends share no state.
Consistent hashing, proposed in 1997, keeps the mapping relatively stable when backends are added or removed, minimizing disruption to existing connections.
Simple connection tracking is usually enough, falling back to consistent hashing when the system is under pressure, such as an ongoing denial of service attack.

title: Packet forwarding in network load balancers
article: doc>sre.google/sre-book/load-balancing-frontend#Load Balancing at the Virtual IP Address

definition.text: A network load balancer can forward a packet to its chosen backend by network address translation, by changing the data link layer destination, or by encapsulating the packet in another IP packet.

facts.text: Network address translation needs a tracking-table entry for every connection, which precludes a completely stateless fallback mechanism.

Changing the destination MAC address lets the backend see the original IP addresses and reply directly to the sender (Direct Server Response), which saves a great deal when replies are large and keeps no state on the balancer.
Layer 2 forwarding needs every balancer and backend in one broadcast domain, which stops working at scale.

Packet encapsulation wraps the packet in a GRE-encapsulated IP packet addressed to the backend, so balancer and backend can be on separate continents, at the price of 24 bytes of overhead that may exceed the MTU.

title: Lame duck state
article: doc>sre.google/sre-book/load-balancing-datacenter#A Robust Approach to Unhealthy Tasks: Lame Duck State

definition.text: A backend in lame duck state is listening and able to serve but explicitly asks clients to stop sending requests, and it broadcasts that fact to all its active clients.

facts.text: From a client's view a backend is healthy and processing requests, refusing connections (starting up, shutting down or abnormal), or in lame duck state.
Inactive clients still send periodic UDP health checks, so lame duck information reaches all clients, typically within 1 or 2 round trips, whatever their state.
The state simplifies clean shutdown, avoiding errors for requests active on tasks being stopped, which eases code pushes, maintenance and restarts after machine failures.
On shutdown the task gets SIGTERM, enters lame duck state and lets ongoing requests drain, then after a configured interval, by rule of thumb 10s to 150s, exits cleanly or is killed.

It also lets clients connect while a backend runs long initialization, with the backend signaling when ready; servers may stay in lame duck state after starting to prewarm until performance is nominal.

A simpler alternative, flow control, treats a backend as unhealthy once a client's active requests reach a limit (100 is reasonable for most), but it protects only against extreme overload and can leave all backends unreachable.

definition.text: Subsetting limits the pool of backend tasks a client connects to, because each connection costs memory and CPU at both ends, and too many connections per client or per backend waste resources for little gain.

facts.text: A typical subset size is 20 to 100 backends; use larger subsets when clients are far fewer than backends, or when clients send bursts and large fan-out, so load spreads over more backends.
The selection algorithm should assign backends uniformly, since overloading one by 10% means overprovisioning all by 10%, and should minimize connection churn across restarts, failures and resizes.
Random subsetting works poorly: with 300 clients, 300 backends and subsets of 10%, the least loaded backend gets 50% of average load and the most loaded 150%; subsets near 75% would be needed.

Deterministic subsetting divides clients into rounds so each round assigns every backend to exactly one client, using a shuffled backend list, and each client takes the subset matching its position in the round.

The list must be shuffled, with a different seed per round, so a failed backend's load spreads over all remaining backends instead of only its subset, and consecutive backends updated together are not one client's whole subset.
In the 300-client example with subsets of 10 backends, deterministic subsetting gives every backend exactly the same number of connections; in general, counts differ by at most 1.

definition.text: Simple round robin sends each client's requests in turn to the connectable, non-lame-duck backends in its subset; it beats random selection but can leave up to a 2x spread in CPU between the least and most loaded task.

facts.text: Clients may issue requests at different rates, especially when very different processes share backends, so with small subsets the backends of the busiest clients are naturally more loaded.

Query costs vary widely: the most expensive requests may use 1000x or more CPU than the cheapest and cannot always be predicted; one Java backend averages about 15 ms of CPU per query yet some need up to 10 seconds.
Machine diversity means the same request is different work on different CPUs; Google modeled CPU rate in a virtual unit (GCU) and had its scheduler scale reservations by machine type.

Unpredictable factors include antagonistic neighbors, which can change performance by up to 20%, and task restarts, which need extra resources for minutes, so servers may stay in lame duck state to prewarm.
Poor in-datacenter balancing artificially limits capacity: you may reserve 1,000 CPUs for a service in a datacenter yet be unable to use more than, say, 700.

definition.text: Least-loaded round robin has each client track its active requests to every backend in its subset and round robin among the backends with the fewest.

facts.text: Loaded tasks tend to have higher latency than those with spare capacity, so the policy naturally moves load away from them; round robin among the minimal set avoids leaving some backends unused.
A seriously unhealthy task may fast-fail with 100% errors and attract traffic because it looks lightly loaded, sinkholing traffic; counting recent errors as active requests fixes this.
The active-request count is a poor proxy for capability, since requests that mostly wait on other backends use little CPU, so a backend twice as fast may look equally loaded.
Each client sees only its own requests, and in practice large services using it see the most loaded backend using twice the CPU of the least loaded, about as poorly as plain round robin.

title: Weighted round robin with backend feedback

definition.text: Weighted round robin uses backend-provided information: each client keeps a capability score per backend and distributes requests round robin in proportion to those scores.

facts.text: Backends include their observed queries per second, errors per second and utilization, typically CPU, in each response, health-check replies included.
Clients periodically adjust capability scores from each backend's successful requests and utilization cost, and failed requests carry a penalty that affects future decisions.
In practice it worked very well, drastically narrowing the spread between the most and least loaded tasks after clients switched from least-loaded round robin.
Policies are hard because clients decide in real time with only partial or stale backend state, and simple ones ignore backend state altogether.
